notes.meaning: Jacob settled down to live in the land of Canaan, where his father Isaac had lived as a visiting stranger. Unlike his brother Esau, who had quickly gained wealth and land in Edom, Jacob stayed in the land of promise. He chose to live by faith and wait patiently for what God had promised.

This starts the family history of Jacob, focusing on his seventeen-year-old son Joseph. Joseph took care of the flocks alongside the sons of his father's secondary wives, Bilhah and Zilpah. When Joseph saw his brothers doing wrong in the fields, he brought an honest report back to Jacob.

Jacob loved Joseph more than all his other children because Joseph was born late in his life, and was the firstborn child of his beloved wife Rachel. Jacob made him a special, ornate robe to honor him above his brothers. This grand garment was a clear sign of deep favoritism and status.

The other brothers realized that their father loved Joseph more than any of them, and this made them deeply bitter. Their resentment grew so strong that they could not even give him a common, friendly greeting. Their open hostility showed just how fractured the family had become.
God gave Joseph a special dream about what would happen in the future. Joseph innocently shared what he had seen with his brothers. Hearing the dream made them hate him even more than before.
Joseph asked his brothers to listen carefully to the dream he had received. He spoke openly, not realizing how much his brothers already resented him.

Joseph described how they were all out in the field tying bundles of grain together. Suddenly, Joseph's bundle stood tall and upright while their bundles gathered around and bowed down to it. This dream pointed forward to a future time when his family would need grain and bow before him.

The brothers quickly figured out the meaning of the dream and took it as a personal insult. They asked in angry disbelief if their younger brother really expected to rule over them. Their jealousy flared up even higher because of the dream and the way he spoke about it.

God gave Joseph a second dream, confirming that the first dream would truly come to pass. Joseph told his brothers that this time he saw the sun, the moon, and eleven stars bowing down to him. These symbols stood for his entire family giving him honor.

Joseph repeated this second dream to his father as well as his brothers. Jacob scolded Joseph to check any growing pride and to help calm the brothers' anger. He asked whether he, Joseph's family mother, and his brothers would really bow down to the earth before him.

The brothers burned with intense envy over what Joseph had told them. Jacob, on the other hand, quietly kept the matter in mind and thought about it often. He knew God sometimes spoke through dreams and wondered how these things might unfold.

Some time later, the older brothers led their father's flocks to find fresh pasture near Shechem. That valley was known for having plenty of green grass and water. It was a long journey of about fifty miles north from where Jacob lived.

Jacob called Joseph and told him he wanted to send him up to Shechem to find his brothers. Joseph answered right away that he was ready to go. Even though his brothers hated him, he obeyed his father without hesitation.

Jacob sent Joseph off from the valley of Hebron to check on his brothers' safety and the health of the flocks. Jacob worried because his sons had previously attacked and killed people in Shechem. Joseph faithfully completed the long trek and arrived at Shechem.
Joseph arrived at Shechem but could not find his family anywhere. As he wandered across the open fields looking for them, a local man noticed him and asked what he was searching for.
Joseph told the stranger that he was looking for his brothers. He asked if the man could tell him where they had moved their flocks to graze.
The man explained that the brothers had packed up and left, saying they were going to Dothan. Dothan was about fifteen miles farther north, but Joseph kept searching until he found them there.

The brothers spotted Joseph approaching in the distance, easily recognizing his special robe. Before he could even reach them, their old hatred flared up into a cold-blooded plan. They immediately began plotting how to murder him.
The brothers mocked Joseph as he walked toward them, calling him a master of dreams. Their cruel sarcasm showed how much they despised the messages God had given him.

They agreed to kill Joseph, drop his body into a dry storage pit, and lie that a wild beast had eaten him. They thought this violent act would destroy his dreams and prove that he would never rule over them.
Reuben, the oldest brother, overheard their deadly plan and stepped in to protect Joseph. He tried to stop them from committing outright murder by telling them not to take his life.

Reuben urged the brothers not to shed blood, but to throw Joseph into an empty pit in the wilderness instead. Reuben said this as a secret rescue plan, intending to slip back later, pull Joseph out, and return him safely to Jacob.

As soon as Joseph walked up to greet them, the brothers attacked him and tore off his robe. Ripping away this fine coat was their way of stripping him of the special standing his father had given him.
They grabbed Joseph and shoved him down into a deep, empty cistern that had no water in it. They left him trapped at the bottom, helpless and crying out in fear, with no way to climb out.

The brothers sat down calmly to eat a meal, showing no pity for Joseph trapped in the pit nearby. While eating, they saw a trading caravan of Ishmaelites on the road from Gilead, carrying valuable spices and oils down toward Egypt.

Judah spoke up and asked what they would actually gain by leaving their brother to die and hiding his blood. He saw a chance to get rid of Joseph, make some money, and avoid the guilt of killing him directly.

Judah urged them to sell Joseph as a slave to the traders instead of putting their own hands on him. He reminded them that Joseph was still their brother and their own flesh. The other brothers agreed that this was a good solution.

When the Midianite traders in the caravan came near, the brothers pulled Joseph out of the cistern. They sold him for twenty silver coins, the going price for a young slave. The traders took Joseph away to Egypt, keeping him alive under God's hidden plan.
Reuben had been away during the sale and returned to the cistern to rescue Joseph secretly. When he looked inside and found it empty, he tore his clothes in deep sorrow and panic.
Reuben hurried back to his brothers, crying out that the boy was gone. As the firstborn son, he knew he was responsible for Joseph's life and had no idea how he could ever face his father again.
To cover up their crime, the brothers slaughtered a young goat and dipped Joseph's robe in its blood. They planned to use this blood to make it look like a wild animal had killed him.

They sent the bloody robe back to Jacob with a cold, deceptive message. They claimed they had simply found it and asked Jacob to look closely to see whether it belonged to his son. They would not even acknowledge Joseph as their brother.

Jacob examined the robe, recognized it immediately, and cried out in agony that a wild animal had eaten Joseph. The brothers' cruel trick worked completely, leaving Jacob convinced that his beloved son had been torn to pieces.
Overcome with sorrow, Jacob tore his clothes and wrapped rough sackcloth around his waist. He spent many days in deep mourning. His public display showed the crushing pain of a brokenhearted father.

All of Jacob's sons and daughters gathered to comfort him, but he refused to let his sorrow be softened. He wept bitterly and declared that he would mourn for Joseph until he went down to Sheol, the place of the dead, to join him.

Far away in Egypt, the traders sold Joseph to Potiphar, an important royal official who commanded Pharaoh's palace guard. Even as a slave in a foreign land, Joseph was placed right where God would later raise him to power.
